'''whitleather''' (hwit′leᴛ̵ʜ″ėr), ''n.'' [Early mod. E. ''whittlether, whitlether;'' < ''white''<sup>1</sup> + ''leather.''] '''1.''' Leather dressed with alum; white leather. See ''leather''.
{{smaller block|<poem>Hast thou so much moisture
In thy ''whit-leather'' hide yet that thou canst cry?</poem>
{{right|''Beau. and Fl.'', Scornful Lady, v. 1.}}}}
'''2.''' The nuchal ligament of grazing animals, as the ox, supporting the head: same as ''paxwax.'' See cut under ''ligamentum.''

'''whitling''' (hwit′ling), ''n.'' [= Sw. ''hvitling'', a whiting; as ''white''<sup>1</sup> + ''-ling''<sup>1</sup>.] The young of the bull-trout. ''Imp. Dict.''

'''whitlow''' (hwit′lō), ''n.'' [A corruption of ''whitflaw, whiteflaw'', for ''whickflaw'', a dial. var. of ''quick-flaw'', perhaps simulating ''white''<sup>1</sup> + ''low''<sup>4</sup>, a fire, as if in ref. to the occasionally white appearance of such swellings, and to the inflammation.] '''1.''' A suppurative inflammation of the deeper tissues of a finger, usually of the terminal phalanx; felon, panaritium, or paronychia.—'''2.''' An inflammatory disease of the feet in sheep. It occurs around the hoof, where an acrid matter collects, which ought to be discharged.

'''whitlowwort''' (hwit′lō-wėrt), ''n.'' See ''Paronychia''<sup>1</sup>, 2 (with cut).

'''Whit-Monday''' (hwit′mun″dā), ''n.'' [< ''whit''<sup>2</sup> (for ''white''<sup>1</sup>) + ''Monday''.] The Monday following Whitsunday. In England the day is generally observed as a holiday. Also called ''Whitsun-Monday''.

'''whitneyite''' (hwit′ni-īt), ''n.'' [Named after J. D. ''Whitney'', an American geologist (born 1819).] A native arsenide of copper, occurring massive, of a reddish-white color and metallic to submetallic luster, and found in the copper region of Lake Superior.

'''whitret''' (hwit′ret), ''n.'' [Sc. also ''quhitred'', ''quhittret'', ''whitrack''; origin uncertain. Cf. E. dial. (Cornwall) ''whitneck'', a white-throated weasel.] A weasel. [Scotch.]

'''Whitson†''', ''n.'' An old form of ''Whitsun''.

'''whitsour''' (hwit′sour), ''n.'' [Appar. < ''white''<sup>1</sup> + ''sour''.] A variety of summer apple.

'''whitster†''', ''n.'' See ''whitester''.

'''whitsul†''' (hwit′sul), ''n.'' [< ''white''<sup>1</sup> + ''soul''<sup>2</sup>, ''sul''.] A dish composed of milk, cheese, curds, and butter.
{{smaller block|Their meat ''whitsull'', as they call it: namely, milke, soure milke, cheese, curds, butter.
{{right|''R. Carew'', Survey of Cornwall, folio 66.}}}}

<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="transcriber" />{{RunningHeader|whitewing|6913|Whitsunday}}</noinclude>lantic coast of the United States. {{smaller|Various plumages of the bird are distinguished by gunners as ''black, gray, May, great May,'' and ''eastern whitewing''; and it has many other local names. See cut under ''velvet.''}} '''2.''' The chaffinch, ''Fringilla cœlebs'': so called from the white bands on the wing.—'''Whitewing doves''', {{smaller|the pigeons of the genus ''Melopelia.'' See ''white-winged.''}}

'''white-winged''' (hwīt′wingd), ''a.'' Having the wings white, wholly or in part: specifying various birds.—'''White-winged blackbird''', {{smaller|the lark-bunting, ''Calamospiza bicolor,'' the male of which is black with a conspicuous white wing-patch. See cut under ''Calamospiza.''}}—'''White-winged coot.''' {{smaller|See ''coot'', 3.}}—'''White-winged crossbill''', {{smaller|''Loxia leucoptera,'' a North American species, the male of which is carmine-red with two white wing-bars on each wing.}}—'''White-winged dove''', {{smaller|''Melopelia leucoptera,'' a pigeon found in southwestern parts of the United States, with a broad oblique white wing-bar. See cut under ''Melopelia.''}}—'''White-winged gull, lark, sandpiper.''' {{smaller|See the nouns.}}—'''White-winged scoter.''' {{smaller|Same as ''whitewing'', 1.}}—'''White-winged snowbird''', {{smaller|a variety of the common black snowbird, ''Junco hiemalis aikeni,'' with white wingbars, found in the mountains of Colorado. Compare cut under ''snowbird.''}}—'''White-winged surf-duck''', {{smaller|the velvet scoter. See ''whitewing'', 1, and cut under ''velvet.''}}

'''whitewood''' (hwīt′wu̇d), ''n.'' A name of a large number of trees or of their white or whitish timber. {{smaller|The whitewoods of North America are the tulip-tree, ''Liriodendron Tulipifera,'' and the basswood, ''Tilia Americana''; also, in Florida, the Guiana plum, ''Drypetes crocea,'' and the wild cinnamon, ''Canella alba'' (see ''Canella''<sup>1</sup>, and ''whitewood bark,'' below). In the West Indies ''Tabebuia Leucoxylon,'' the whitewood cedar, and ''T. pentaphylla,'' both formerly classed under ''Tecoma,'' are so named, together with ''Ocotea Leucoxylon'' and the white sweetwood, ''Nectandra Antilliana'' (''N. leucantha'' of Grisebach). The cheesewood, ''Pittosporum bicolor,'' of Victoria and Tasmania, and ''Lagunaria Patersoni,'' a small soft-wooded malvaceous tree, found in Queensland and Norfolk Island, are so named; and a large handsome tree, ''Panax elegans'', of eastern Australia, is the mowbulan whitewood. Locally, in England, the linden, ''Tilia Europæa'', and the wayfaring-tree, ''Viburnum Lantana'', and in Cheshire all timber but oak, are called ''whitewood''. (''Britten and Holland''.)—'''White-wood bark,''' the white cinnamon, the bark of ''Canella alba''.}}

'''whiteworm''' (hwīt′wėrm), ''n.'' Same as ''white-grub''.

'''whitewort''' (whīt′wėrt), ''n.'' An old name of the feverfew, ''Chrysanthemum Parthenium'', and of the Solomon’s-seal, ''Polygonatum multiflorum''.

'''whitflaw†''' (hwit′flâ), ''n.'' Same as ''whiteflaw'', ''whitlow'', ''whickflaw''.

'''whither''' (hwiᴛ̵ʜ′ėr), ''adv.'' and ''conj.''   [Formerly also ''whether''; with change of orig. ''d'' to ''th'', as in ''hither'', ''thither'', ''father'', etc.; < ME. ''whider'', ''whidir'', ''whidur'', ''whedir'', ''hwider'', ''whoder'', ''woder'', ''qvider'', ''qvedur'', ''hweder'', whither, < AS. ''hwider'', ''hwyder'', to what place, whither, = Goth. ''hwadre'', whither; < Teut. *''hwa'', who, + compar. suffix ''-der'', ''-ther'': see ''who'', and cf. ''whether''<sup>1</sup> and the correlative adverbs ''hither'' and ''thither''.]   '''I.''' ''interrog. adv.'' '''1.''' To what place?
{{smaller block|Gentill knyghtes, ''whether'' ar ye a-wey?
{{right|''Merlin'' (E. E. T. S.), ii. 245.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>''Whither'' is fled the visionary gleam?
Where is it now, the glory and the dream?</poem>
{{right|''Wordsworth'', Intimations of Mortality, st. 4.}}}}
'''2†.''' To what point or degree? how far? [Rare.]
{{smaller block|''Whither'' at length wilt thou abuse our patience?
{{right|''B. Jonson'', Catiline, iv. 2.}}}}
'''II.''' ''rel. conj.'' '''1.''' To which place.
{{smaller block|<poem>Sothly, soth it is a selcouthe, me thinkes,
''Whider'' that lady is went and wold no lenger dwelle.</poem>
{{right|''William of Palerne'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 701.}}}}

{{smaller block|<poem>Then they fled
Into this abbey, ''whither'' we pursued them.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', C. of E., v. 1. 155.}}}}
{{smaller block|From this countrey towards the South there is a certeine port called Scirings hall, ''whither'' he sayth that a man was not able to Saile in a moneths space, if he lay still by night, although he had euery day a full winde.
{{right|''Hakluyt’s Voyages'', p. 6.}}}}
{{smaller block|What will all the gain of this world signifie in that State ''whither'' we are all hastening apace?
{{right|''Stillingfleet'', Sermons, I. xii.}}}}
'''2.''' Whithersoever.
{{smaller block|Nor let your Chyldren go ''whether'' they will, but know whether they goe, in what company, and what they haue done, good or euill. {{right|''Babees Book'' (E. E. T. S.), p. 64.}}}}
{{smaller block|Thou shalt let her go ''whither'' she will. {{right|Deut. xxi. 14.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>A fool go with thy soul, ''whither'' it goes!</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', 1 Hen. IV., v. 3. 22.}}}}
{{smaller block|''Where'' has now to a considerable extent taken the place, in conversational use, of ''whither'': thus, it would seem rather stilted to say “''whither'' are you going?” instead of “''where'' are you going?” ''Whither'' is still used, however, in the more elevated or serious style, or when precision is required.}}

'''Any whither†.''' See ''anywhither.''
{{smaller block|<poem>Yee haue heard that two Flemings togider
Will vndertake or they goe ''any whither'',
Or they rise once to drinke a Ferkin full
Of good Beerekin. {{right|''Hakluyt’s Voyages'', I. 192.}}</poem>}}
{{smaller block|Wood and water he would fetch vs, guide vs ''any whether''.
{{right|Quoted in ''Capt. John Smith’s'' Works, I. 184.}}}}

'''No whither.''' See ''nowhither.''
{{smaller block|Elisha said unto him, Whence comest thou, Gehazi? And he said, Thy servant went ''no whither''. {{right|2. Ki. v. 25.}}}}

'''whither-out†''' (hwiᴛ̵ʜ′ėr-out), ''interrog. adv.'' and ''rel. conj.'' In what direction outward; whence and whither.

{{smaller block|“Lorde,” quod I, “if any wiȝte wyte ''whider-oute'' it groweth!”
{{right|''Piers Plowman'' (B), xvi. 12.}}}}

'''whithersoever''' (hwiᴛ̵ʜ′ėr-sọ-ev′ėr), ''adv.''   [< ''whither'' + ''soever''.]   To whatever place.

{{smaller block|Master, I will follow thee ''whithersoever'' thou goest.
{{right|Mat. viii. 19.}}}}

'''whitherward''' (hwiᴛ̵ʜ′ėr-wärd), ''interrog. adv.'' and ''rel. conj.''   [< ME. ''whiderward'', ''hwuderward'', ''whoderward''; < ''whither'' + ''-ward''.]   Toward what or which direction or place. [Obsolete or archaic.]

{{smaller block|And asked of hire ''whiderward'' she wente.
{{right|''Chaucer'', Franklin’s Tale, l. 782.}}}}
{{smaller block|''Whitherward'' wentest thou?
{{right|''William Morris'', Sigurd, iii.}}}}

'''whiting<sup>1</sup>''' (hwī′ting), ''n.''   [< ME. ''whytynge''; verbal n. of ''white<sup>1</sup>'', ''v.'']   Chalk which has been dried either in the air or in a kiln, and afterward ground, levigated, and again dried. {{smaller|In trade it has various names, according to the amount of labor expended on it to make it fine and free from grit, there being ordinary or commercial whiting, then Spanish white, then gilders’ whiting, and finally Paris white, which is the best grade. Whiting is used in fine whitewashing, in distemper painting, cleaning plate, making putty, as an adulterant in various processes, as a base for picture-moldings, etc. Also ''whitening''.}}

{{smaller block|When the father hath gotten thousands by the sacrilegious impropriation, the son perhaps may give him [the vicar] a cow’s grass, or a matter of forty shillings per annum; or bestow a little ''whiting'' on the church, and a wainscot seat for his own worship.
{{right|''Rev. T. Adams'', Works, I. 144.}}}}

{{smaller block|When you clean your plate, leave the ''whiting'' plainly to be seen in all the chinks, for fear your lady should not believe you had cleaned it.
{{right|''Swift'', Advice to Servants (Butler).}}}}

'''whiting'''<sup>2</sup> (hwī′ting), ''n.''   [< ME. ''whytynge'' (= MD. ''wijtingh'', ''wittingh'' = MLG. ''witink'', also ''witik'', ''witeke''); < ''white''<sup>1</sup> + ''-ing''<sup>3</sup>.]   '''1.''' A gadoid fish of Europe, ''Merlangus vulgaris'', or another of this genus. {{smaller|It abounds on the British coast, and is highly esteemed for food. It is commonly from 12 to 18 inches}}
{{smaller|long, and of one or two pounds weight, though it grows much larger. It is readily distinguished from the haddock and some other related fishes by the absence of a barbule. The flesh is of a pearly whiteness.}}
{{smaller block|<poem>And here ’s a chain of ''whitings''’ eyes for pearls;
A muscle-monger would have made a better.</poem>
{{right|''Fletcher'', Rule a Wife, iv. 1.}}}}
'''2.''' In the United States, one of several sciænoid fishes of the genus ''Menticirrus'', as ''M. americanus''. The silver whiting, or surf-whiting, is ''M. littoralis''.—'''3.''' The silver hake, ''Merlucius bilinearis''.—'''4.''' The menhaden.—{{smaller|'''Bermuda, bull-head,''' or '''Carolina whiting.''' See ''kingfish'' (''a'').—'''Whiting’s-eye,''' a wistful glance; a leer, or amorous look.}}
{{smaller block|I saw her just now give him the languishing Eye, as they call it; that is, the ''Whiting’s-Eye'', of old called the Sheep’s-Eye.
{{right|''Wycherley'', Gentleman Dancing-Master, iv. 1.}}}}
'''whiting-mop†''' (hwī′ting-mop), ''n.''   [< ''whiting''<sup>2</sup> + ''mop''<sup>1</sup>.]   '''1.''' A young whiting.
{{smaller block|They will swim you their measures, like ''whiting-mops'', as if their feet were fins, and the hinges of their knees oiled. {{right|''Fletcher'' (''and another''), Love’s Cure, ii. 2.}}}}
'''2.''' Figuratively, a fair lass; a pretty girl.
{{smaller block|<poem>I have a stomach, and would content myself
With this pretty ''whiting-mop''.</poem>
{{right|''Massinger'', Guardian, iv. 2.}}}}

[[File:century v08 p0717 c2f1.png|center|331px]]
{{c|{{smaller|Whiting (''Merlangus vulgaris''), one sixth natural size.}}}}

'''whiting-pollack''' (hwī′ting-pol″a̤k), ''n.'' See ''pollack''.

'''whiting-pout''' (hwī′ting-pout), ''n.'' A gadoid fish, the bib, ''Gadus luscus''.

'''whiting-time†''' (hwī′ting-tīm), ''n.'' Bleaching-time.   ''Shak.'', M. W. of W., iii. 3. 140.

'''whitish''' (hwī′tish), ''a.''   [< ME. ''whitisshe''; < ''white''<sup>1</sup> + ''-ish''<sup>1</sup>.]   Somewhat white; white in a moderate degree; albescent.
{{smaller block|His taste is goode, and ''whitisshe'' his coloure.
{{right|''Palladius'', Husbondrie (E. E. T. S.), p. 91.}}}}
{{smaller block|In stooping he saw, about a yard off, something ''whitish'' and square lying on the dark grass. This was an ornamental note-book of pale leather stamped with gold.
{{right|''George Eliot'', Felix Holt, xiii.}}}}

'''whitishness''' (hwī′tish-nes), ''n.'' The quality of being somewhat white; albescence.
{{smaller block|You may more easily make the experiment, by taking good venereal vitriol of a deep blue, and comparing with some of the entire crystals . . . some of the subtile powder of the same salt, which will comparatively exhibit a very considerable degree of ''whitishness.''
{{right|''Boyle'', Exper. Hist. of Colours, II. i. 12.}}}}

'''whitleather''' (hwit′leᴛ̵ʜ″ėr), ''n.''   [Early mod. E. ''whittlether, whitlether;'' < ''white''<sup>1</sup> + ''leather.'']   '''1.''' Leather dressed with alum; white leather. See ''leather''.
{{smaller block|<poem>Hast thou so much moisture
In thy ''whit-leather'' hide yet that thou canst cry?</poem>
{{right|''Beau. and Fl.'', Scornful Lady, v. 1.}}}}
'''2.''' The nuchal ligament of grazing animals, as the ox, supporting the head: same as ''paxwax.'' See cut under ''ligamentum.''

'''whitling''' (hwit′ling), ''n.''   [= Sw. ''hvitling'', a whiting; as ''white''<sup>1</sup> + ''-ling''<sup>1</sup>.]   The young of the bull-trout.   ''Imp. Dict.''

'''whitlow''' (hwit′lō), ''n.''   [A corruption of ''whitflaw, whiteflaw'', for ''whickflaw'', a dial. var. of ''quick-flaw'', perhaps simulating ''white''<sup>1</sup> + ''low''<sup>4</sup>, a fire, as if in ref. to the occasionally white appearance of such swellings, and to the inflammation.]   '''1.''' A suppurative inflammation of the deeper tissues of a finger, usually of the terminal phalanx; felon, panaritium, or paronychia.—'''2.''' An inflammatory disease of the feet in sheep. It occurs around the hoof, where an acrid matter collects, which ought to be discharged.

'''whitlow-grass''' (hwit′lō-grȧs), ''n.'' Originally, either of two early-blooming little plants, ''Saxifraga trydactylites'' and ''Draba verna'' (''Erophila vulgaris''), regarded as curing whitlow. {{smaller|In later times the name has been confined to ''Draba verna'' (vernal ''whitlow-grass''), and thence extended to the whole genus. The section ''Erophila'', however, of this genus, to which ''D. verna'' belongs, is now separated as an independent genus. See ''Draba'', and cut under ''silicle''.}}

'''whitlowwort''' (hwit′lō-wėrt), ''n.'' See ''Paronychia''<sup>1</sup>, 2 (with cut).

'''Whit-Monday''' (hwit′mun″dā), ''n.''   [< ''whit''<sup>2</sup> (for ''white''<sup>1</sup>) + ''Monday''.]   The Monday following Whitsunday. In England the day is generally observed as a holiday. Also called ''Whitsun-Monday''.

'''whitneyite''' (hwit′ni-īt), ''n.''   [Named after J. D. ''Whitney'', an American geologist (born 1819).]   A native arsenide of copper, occurring massive, of a reddish-white color and metallic to submetallic luster, and found in the copper region of Lake Superior.

'''whitret''' (hwit′ret), ''n.''   [Sc. also ''quhitred'', ''quhittret'', ''whitrack''; origin uncertain. Cf. E. dial. (Cornwall) ''whitneck'', a white-throated weasel.]   A weasel. [Scotch.]

'''Whitson†''', ''n.'' An old form of ''Whitsun''.

'''whitsour''' (hwit′sour), ''n.''   [Appar. < ''white''<sup>1</sup> + ''sour''.]   A variety of summer apple.

'''whitster†''', ''n.'' See ''whitester''.

'''whitsul†''' (hwit′sul), ''n.''   [< ''white''<sup>1</sup> + ''soul''<sup>2</sup>, ''sul''.]   A dish composed of milk, cheese, curds, and butter.
{{smaller block|Their meat ''whitsull'', as they call it: namely, milke, soure milke, cheese, curds, butter.
{{right|''R. Carew'', Survey of Cornwall, folio 66.}}}}

'''Whitsun''' (hwit′sun), ''a.''   [Formerly also ''Whitson'', also ''Whisson'', ''Wheeson''; < ME. ''whitson-'', ''wyttson-'' ''whysson-'' (= Icel. ''Hvīta sunna''), Whitsun; abbr. of ''Whitsunday'' or the common first element of ''Whitsunday'', ''Whitsun-week'', etc.]   Of, pertaining to, or observed at Whitsuntide; following Whitsunday, or falling in Whitsun-week: generally used in composition: as, ''Whitsun''-ale; ''Whitsun''-Monday, etc.—'''Whitsun day.''' {{smaller|See ''Whitsunday.''}}

'''Whitsun-ale''' (hwit′sun-āl), ''n.''   [Also ''Whitson-ale''; < ''Whitsun'' + ''ale.'']   A festival formerly held in England at Whitsuntide by the inhabitants of the various parishes, who met generally in or near a large barn in the vicinity of the church, ate and drank, and engaged in various games and sports.
{{smaller block|May-games, Wakes, and ''Whitson-ales'', &c., if they be not at unseasonable hours, may justly be permitted.
{{right|''Burton'', Anat. of Mel., p. 276.}}}}

'''Whitsunday''' (hwit′sun-dā), ''n.''   [< ME. ''whitsunday'', ''whith sounday'', ''witsondai'', ''wisson-day'', ''hwite sune-dei'', ''hwite sune-dai'', etc., < AS. ''hwīta sunnan-dæg'', only in dat. case ''hwītan sunnan dæg'' (= Icel. ''hvītasunnu-dagr'' (cf. also ''hwīta-dagar'', ‘white days,’ a name for Whitsun-week, ''hvīta-daga-vika'', ‘white days-week,’ ''hvīta-sunnudags-vika'', Whitsunday’s week) = Norw. ''Kvitsunndag'', Whitsunday), < ''hwīt'', white, + ''sunnandæg'', Sunday: see ''white''<sup>1</sup> and ''Sunday''. The name refers to the white garments (Icel. ''hvīta-vādhir'', white weeds) worn by candidates for baptism. The notion which has been current that ''Whitsunday'' is derived from the G. ''pfingsten'', Pentecost (see ''Pinkster'' and ''Pente-''<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
